title: Russia was not ready for the data center war it started with Ukraine
gist: After Russia attacked Ukrainian data centers in late September, Ukrainian drones struck three of Yandex's largest data centers on October 8, 9 and 11, causing outages across Russian payments, banking, e-commerce and cloud services and hitting supercomputers used to train YandexGPT. Pro-Kremlin bloggers say Russia's hypercentralized, sovereign-internet-constrained infrastructure is more vulnerable than Ukraine's decentralized, cloud-backed one.

themes.theme: Ukrainian strikes on Yandex data centers

insights.claim: Ukrainian drones hit three Yandex data centers in four days: Sasovo on October 8, Kaluga on October 9 (one of Russia's largest, 63 MW maximum), and Vladimir on October 11, which forced Yandex to suspend operations there.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Data centers are now explicit wartime targets, a risk factor for digital-infrastructure operators in conflict zones.
insights.locator: The first Ukrainian drone attack damaged a data center

insights.claim: The Sasovo and Vladimir sites house Yandex's three Nvidia A100-based supercomputers used for YandexGPT training: Chervonenkis at 29.42 petaflops (Top 500 rank 101), Lyapunov at 20.03 (rank 161) and Galushkin at 20.64 (rank 134); damage to the Sasovo ones was unclear.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Russian domestic AI training capacity relies on aging A100 hardware that is hard to replace under sanctions.
insights.locator: The first Ukrainian drone attack damaged a data center in the Sasovo region

insights.claim: Ukrainian President Zelenskyy described the strikes on Yandex as a symmetrical response to Russia's attacks on Ukrainian data centers and mobile networks, which disrupted service for up to 100,000 Kyiv households.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Tit-for-tat targeting of digital infrastructure is escalating alongside energy-grid strikes.
insights.locator: But Ukraine soon began striking back

insights.claim: Damage to Yandex data centers has reportedly interrupted Russian payment apps, digital banking, email, e-commerce, streaming, ride-hailing, food delivery and mapping, and also its cloud, whose customers include large grocery and fast-food chains; Yandex search has about 70 percent market share.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Concentration in one provider converts a few physical hits into economy-wide outages, a single-point-of-failure risk.

insights.claim: Milblogger Ratio Militaris says Yandex's hypercentralization, both as a market monopolist and in concentrating its capacity in a few large nodes, has turned a past Russian advantage into a wartime weakness.
insights.speaker: Ratio Militaris
insights.so_what: Pro-Kremlin voices themselves flag fragility, suggesting domestic pressure for decentralization investment.
insights.locator: Yandex and the digital ecosystem it created

insights.claim: Russia's 2019 Sovereign Internet Law has effectively prevented Russian companies from using infrastructure even in friendly countries, so replicating infrastructure in Belarus or Kazakhstan is virtually impossible and capacity there is insufficient; China might work but would need legislative changes.
insights.speaker: Artjockey
insights.so_what: Regulatory isolation limits resilience options, which could favor China-based hosting if rules change.
insights.locator: Russian companies like Yandex will also have a hard time

insights.claim: Russians may wait up to six months for Yandex to replace damaged data center equipment, per an unnamed IT expert in Kommersant, comparable to Amazon's long recovery after Iranian drone strikes on data centers in Bahrain and the UAE earlier this year.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Extended repair times imply prolonged service degradation and a hardware supply bottleneck under sanctions.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, Russians may be waiting up to six months

insights.claim: Ukraine's digital ecosystem consists of smaller, decentralized data centers with backup infrastructure, including equipment moved underground or abroad, and commentators suggest it may prove more resilient than Russia's in continued exchanges.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Decentralized architecture is a template for wartime digital resilience, relevant to infrastructure and cloud-sovereignty plays.
insights.locator: By comparison, Ukraine has a much more decentralized

insights.claim: Microsoft and Amazon provided free cloud services to migrate Ukrainian government services to Europe, and AWS alone hosts over 15 petabytes of data from more than 60 Ukrainian government organizations plus data from the energy company DTEK.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Hyperscalers are de facto custodians of a wartime state's digital continuity, strengthening their geopolitical role.
insights.locator: Western tech giants like Microsoft and Amazon
